prompt:
Write an opinion piece of about 800 words on whether cities should remove minimum parking requirements from their planning rules. Take a side and argue for it.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Write mostly medium-length, complete sentences.

text:
Cities should scrap their minimum parking requirements, and they should do it soon. The rules are a relic of mid-century planning that assumed every household would own cars and every destination would be reached by driving, and they have quietly shaped American cities in ways that few residents ever chose. Removing them does not ban parking. It simply returns the decision to the people who actually pay for it and use it.

Consider what a minimum requirement does in practice. A city council decides that every apartment must come with one and a half spaces, or that a restaurant needs one space for every hundred square feet of dining room. Those numbers usually come from manuals that surveyed suburban sites with ample free parking, and they are often applied to dense urban neighborhoods where the same logic makes no sense. A developer who wants to build twenty homes on a small lot may find that the parking mandate eats half the site, forcing either a smaller building or an expensive underground garage. Either way, the cost is passed along, and the people who bear it include those who never owned a car.

That cost is large and mostly invisible. Structured parking can run tens of thousands of dollars per space to build, and underground spaces cost even more. Those expenses are folded into rents and purchase prices, so a household without a car ends up subsidizing storage for the cars of its neighbors. Researchers have estimated that parking requirements raise the price of housing meaningfully, and the effect falls hardest on the lowest-income renters, who are also the households least likely to own a vehicle. A rule that claims to serve the public by guaranteeing convenience is in fact making homes more expensive for the people who can least afford them.

The requirements also damage the places they are meant to serve. Every mandated space takes up land that could hold housing, shops, or workplaces, and it spreads destinations farther apart, which makes walking and transit less practical and driving more necessary. Old main streets that were built before parking minimums often have the most vibrant street life, and many of those buildings could not legally be built today. A bakery in a historic downtown storefront would be impossible under current rules, because there is no room for the lot out front. When cities require parking, they are effectively outlawing the kind of neighborhoods that people pay a premium to visit on vacation.

Defenders of the rules raise a reasonable worry, which is that without mandates, new buildings will push their cars onto neighboring streets and leave residents circling for a spot. This fear is real, but it has a better answer than a blanket requirement. Cities can manage curb space directly by pricing it, issuing permits for residents, and returning the revenue to the neighborhood. Pricing the curb is a far more precise tool than forcing every developer to guess at demand in advance, and it treats scarce street space as something of value rather than something to give away. Where the curb is managed well, new buildings with little parking tend not to cause the chaos that critics predict.

It also helps to remember that removing a minimum is not the same as removing parking. Developers will still build it wherever there is demand for it, because tenants and customers want it and lenders often insist on it. What changes is that the amount becomes a business decision rather than a legal one. A suburban shopping center on a highway will probably keep a large lot, and nothing about reform prevents that. A building near a train station might build far fewer spaces and offer the savings as lower rents. The market can sort out which is which far better than a rulebook written decades ago.

The evidence from cities that have tried this is encouraging. Several American cities, including Buffalo, Minneapolis, and Anchorage, along with a growing number of others, have eliminated or sharply reduced their requirements in recent years. Early results suggest that developers continue to provide parking where it is needed, while some projects that would once have been infeasible are now being built. The sky has not fallen, and the neighborhoods that moved first are not suffering the shortages that opponents warned about. As more places follow, the data will get better, but the direction is already clear.

There is also a fairness argument that deserves more weight than it usually gets. Parking requirements force everyone to pay for a service that only some use, and they do so through the price of everything from groceries to rent. Few of us would accept a rule that bundled the cost of a gym membership into every apartment lease, yet we tolerate the equivalent for car storage. Ending the mandate lets people buy the amount of parking they actually want, no more and no less.

Cities should also recognize that this reform costs them almost nothing. It requires no new spending, no new agency, and no complicated program, only the deletion of a few lines from the zoning code. For a change that could lower housing costs, revive walkable streets, and give residents real choices, that is an unusually good bargain. The minimums have had their trial, and the results are in. It is time for councils to repeal them and let neighborhoods build what they actually need.
